analysis.one_liner: Directs the FCC to monitor cellular carriers' prices and consider licensing more competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after its sponsor introduced it and one subcommittee was assigned, no further action was taken before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1991 the FCC licensed only two cellular carriers in each market, a duopoly. This bill would have required the FCC to open a formal inquiry into whether that structure delivered high-quality service at cost-based rates, publish carriers' charges, profit rates, and cost-allocation practices, require annual independent compliance audits, and consider licensing additional carriers in the top 30 markets and applying telephone-style accounting rules to cellular companies. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Telecommunications Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Cellular customers — including rural users — who would gain from public price and profit data, service quality standards, possible rate discipline through cost-based rate scrutiny, and potentially more carriers competing in the largest markets. State utility commissions would also gain access to carriers' books for audits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cell phone customers and state regulators

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FCC to initiate a proceeding within 60 days of enactment and finish it within 9 months to determine whether current policy ensures high-quality cellular service at reasonable cost-based rates in rural and urban areas.
Requires the FCC to obtain and make public cellular carriers' wholesale and retail charges, cost allocation and depreciation practices, terms of service, and rates of return on investment and equity.

Directs the FCC to consider licensing additional facilities-based carriers in at least the top 30 cellular markets by January 1, 1993, breaking up the two-carrier-per-market structure licensed since 1982.

Directs the FCC to consider annual independent audits of carriers' cost compliance, with public release and giving state commissions access to carriers' books and records, and to consider separate wholesale and retail operations with arm's-length dealings between them.

Requires a report to Congress within one year, signed by all sitting FCC Commissioners, analyzing competition in cellular and recommending whether each proposed policy would serve the public interest.

analysis.who_pays: The two licensed cellular carriers in each market, which would face public disclosure of charges and profit margins, annual audits, possible accounting rules, and the prospect of new licensed competitors in the top 30 markets. The FCC would bear the cost of running the inquiry and ongoing monitoring docket.

drawbacks.text: The bill itself requires no new rules — it only mandates an inquiry and a report, so it could have produced a year of paperwork without lowering any bills or adding any competitors.

Applying telephone-style uniform accounting and cost-allocation rules to a young, fast-changing industry could have imposed compliance costs that carriers passed through to customers, a concern underlying the industry's later move to less regulated treatment.
Mandating separate wholesale and retail operations for every licensee, even small rural carriers, could have been burdensome relative to the competitive benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a low-cost, transparency-first response to a two-carrier cellular market: its main tools were public data, audits, and a study of whether to license more competitors. The main honest objection is that it mandated study rather than action, so its benefits depended on the FCC and a later Congress acting on the findings. It died without any committee action, so none of its costs or benefits ever materialized.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Bilbray introduced the bill on April 10, 1991, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on April 22, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance.
No further action was recorded for the rest of the 102nd Congress, which ended January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The two licensed cellular carriers in each market, which were never subjected to the bill's public pricing and profit disclosures, audits, or the prospect of additional licensed competitors in the top 30 markets.

for.name: Rep. James H. Bilbray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the FCC to monitor cellular carriers and consider licensing more competitors; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Telecommunications and Finance Subcommittee, and never reported it out or scheduled any action.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested; the outcome was decided by committee inaction rather than a recorded split.

industries.note: Under the 1982 licensing decision, only two carriers were licensed per market, giving them protected regional duopolies. The bill would have made their charges and profit rates public, required independent audits and possible telephone-style accounting, and could have added licensed competitors in the top 30 markets — costs borne by the carriers and potential savings for customers. Its death left the duopoly structure untouched.

The bill would have required the FCC to run a formal inquiry within fixed deadlines, maintain an ongoing monitoring docket, and report to Congress — new workload, but also new data and authority over an industry it had licensed only thinly. The requirement that the report be signed by all sitting Commissioners would have put each Commissioner's position on the record.
